doc.title: Kent Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 22, 2006

title: Loss and recovery in New Orleans after the storm
summary: Family homes lost, musicians leaving, the city's history and rebuilding, and lost photographs.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: of my house and that was it, you know, decorative tiles on my roof. That was it. I mean I was thankful. I mean in relation to everybody else who lost everything. My parents lost their houses, my sisters lost their houses, only one brother, believe it or not who lived in a part of town that really flooded but his house was fine. But it was unbelievable, truly. I mean until you see it for yourself or saw it for yourself during that time you would have thought an atomic bomb had been dropped in New Orleans, it was just that bad when I came back. But now the city is in a recovery mode. And actually part of my teaching was that I said well let me go back to see how I can help the city deal with what we’ve lost because we truly lost a lot of musicians. I mean there’s people like the Nevilles who say they’re never going back. Some of them say that they’re not going to go back. And so we are at a crossroads for lack of a better definition in terms of our culture, in terms of our infrastructure, in terms of where we are, where we were then, even where we are now, how do we rebuild. That question as you know is sort of still being flushed out there. And so to make a long story short or a short story longer, we’re in a very interesting place right now in terms of the city. And maybe this might be one of those statements, you know, as New Orleans goes maybe as America will follow. What do we value? What do we really truly value about — I think our individuality, about our music, about a lot of things. In this conversation a lot has been lost because even though you might hear about the kind of poverty that existed in New Orleans during Katrina, which was terrible and you have to acknowledge that, the educational system, breakdown in infrastructure, a lot of people don’t realize that New Orleans was where one of the first operas was performed in the United States. Obviously you know the birth of jazz. It was an investment banking center at one time, one of our most important ports. There was a lot of history that happened in New Orleans that we sort of forget about in terms of the birth of this nation you know. And it’s sort of like in this renaissance or this rebirth that we have to go through I hope that the United States understands that New Orleans still has something to offer. Now what that is we have to define that in terms of how we grow out of this. Because it’s going to be a growth process, I’m telling you. I mean you know maybe you go down there and you really see it for yourself because it’s still, in some way, I don’t know if you saw the Spike Lee film or saw portions of it, but it is really a devastating experience just to see entire neighborhoods wiped off the face of the earth you know. And for me you just have to say well what can I do? What can I think or what can I do creatively? You know and that’s sort of like — which is interesting about the situation where we are in now because we did the camp in New Orleans and we had half the students, and now we’re up here teaching kids. So you know we’ll still have something to offer. All is not lost. But it is a really wrenching kind of a thing, just for people who have seriously lost everything. And I mean sometimes we think about it in terms of the © Fillius Jazz Archive -23-

material possessions. But I’ll give you an example. Entire families have lost photographs. So how do you — you know what I mean? How do you give that back to somebody? You know you can give them a house, you can give them a car, you can give them all the things that make them function, but when they sit back and they start talking about the photographs that they lost or the house where they grew up in that their mothers, grandfathers and you’ve done all these things. You know what I mean? That’s something, that emotional tie that you have to figure it out. You have to figure it out because there was something lost but then there’s something that has to be either gained or regained again. And that’s sort of like what we’re going through right now.
Well probably it definitely will be different and I hope it’s better.
I hope it comes out with a character, like you said, maybe the country can follow the character of that place somehow.
